single_points.text: One reviewer says that starting a profession requires grinding gold first.

citation.review_text:
Incredible World, Wasted Potential – Grinding Instead of Enjoying the Game

I genuinely wanted to love Red Dead Online. And honestly, that is what makes this so disappointing.

Rockstar created one of the most beautiful, detailed, and immersive open worlds in gaming history. The atmosphere, wildlife, landscapes, and attention to detail are absolutely incredible. The potential for a living, breathing multiplayer world is enormous.

I came into Red Dead Online expecting to explore the world, hunt animals, meet other players, earn money, and gradually build my own life as a trader or moonshiner.

Instead, I discovered that even basic gameplay mechanics, such as starting a profession, are locked behind an exhausting grind.

Want to become a trader? Grind gold first.

Want to start producing moonshine? Grind even more gold.

Want to experience the different professions and activities this beautiful world has to offer? Prepare to spend hours repeating activities you might not even enjoy, just to unlock the content you actually came to play.

**At some point, the game stops feeling like entertainment and starts feeling like a second job.**

And that is genuinely sad.

I don't mind progression. I don't mind working towards something meaningful in a game. In fact, I enjoy building businesses, developing characters, and gradually improving my equipment.

But there is a massive difference between rewarding progression and forcing players to grind repetitive activities just to access fundamental gameplay systems.

I don't want everything handed to me for free. I want to earn my progress by actually playing the profession I've chosen, not by grinding unrelated game modes for hours before I'm even allowed to start.

What makes this particularly frustrating is that the world itself is already there. The hunting systems, towns, wildlife, transportation, beautiful environments, and multiplayer infrastructure already exist.

The foundation for an incredibl…

cohorts.summary: Mid-tier players accept restrictive mission design and harsh saving limits as part of the massive experience.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the saving system features only a single autosave with no backup files, which can cause players to lose progress, items, or horses upon dying or interruption.

citations.review_text: Did Billy Midnight mission. Horse I loved and wanted to use for the rest of the game ran into the train for some reason and died. Game didn't tell me. Walk back to Rhodes because I can't whistle for it at that range. Horse is dead on the train tracks. No save to go back to without losing 4 hours of progress because there's only one autosave at a time and it autosaved immediately after I finished Billy Midnight, so the horse is already dead. This and several other bad and otherwise completely unnecessary design choices that make the game either take ages to do anything or just make it generally a hassle.

The game is good, but I wouldn't recommend it because of its saving system and anti-cheat design.

Having only one autosave with no backup files can easily result in losing your progress, horse, or cash, or having to redo quests because of a mistake, glitch, or simply forgetting to pause the game when someone rings your doorbell and you need to step away.

Not being able to save your game because you've been cheating is hilarious. Rockstar Games acts like a bunch of children, desperately protecting achievements and trophies in a single-player open-world game. Let people play however they want, they paid for it.

Thankfully, there are trainers and mods that let you cheat, and eventually, you'll end up using them after getting fed up with these restrictions.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe missions as restrictive and heavily reliant on following waypoints and checking the minimap, offering little freedom of approach.

citations.review_text: It's a good game - but there are some caveats. Rockstar's game design is a bit antiquated and the missions don't give the amount of freedom you think that they should. It forces you into a cycle of chasing waypoints and constantly checking your minimap to follow directions. Personally, I don't like that much hand-holding in video games, I wish there was a way to dial it back. But, overall, it's a solid package that runs well and looks great.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is one of those games that makes you forget you're playing a game. The incredible open world, amazing characters, realistic details, and emotional story make it an unforgettable experience. Just riding your horse through the wilderness, hunting, exploring, or watching the sunset can be just as enjoyable as the main missions. The attention to detail is absolutely insane, and the world feels alive in a way few games can match. The pacing can be a little slow at times, and some missions feel quite restrictive, but the overall experience is worth every minute.

citations.review_text:
Easily one of if not THE best story games ever. Great characters with their own stories and progression, fun sidequests and optional things like hunting and robbing places, fantastic open world with cool secrets and stuff to find. If you want it, Red Dead 2 probably has it. 

The only real issue I had with it was I felt the story was a little bit slow from the beginning to about chapter 2-3, but I would say that is like complaining about the early seasons of the hit show Better Call Saul, as they both are important for character progression and the later parts would not be NEARLY as good without them.

9.7/10

A game of hardship, the American dream, trauma, and heartbreak. I am constantly compelled by this games narrative and character development. A must play for anyone who likes open world games. The only thing to keep note of is that it is a very slowly paced game, especially in the beginning. But once you get used to that, you will discover a gem

citations.review_text: Thanks rockstar, I bought your game but now I can’t play it since “my account doesn’t own the game” and your support won’t tell me why.

I'm only giving a thumbs-down because of the Rockstar Launcher. There's no way this act of "protest" will actually mean anything to TakeTwo, but a boy can dream I suppose.
Now as for my actual review about the 4th best selling game of all time that nobody will care about: This game is very good. It manages to compact every Western trope and theme in existence into its story with the best performances I've ever seen from a videogame outside of TLoU. These characters are so well-written, well-acted, well-modeled, and well-animated that they genuinely feel like real people that you want to love. The attention to detail in general is something to behold. Outside of the gorgeous environments and teeming wildlife, every single item and area of the game feels like a true reflection of 1899. Still, this commitment to realism is one of the game's biggest drawbacks. Given how much the developers have clearly invested in making this world feel real, it's sticks out when it backslides into videogame logic. NPC's are the most jarring symptom of this. 
They'll often get mad at you for sprinting in front of them, for example. Sure, that's what a real person might do, but I'm not going to take the situation seriously if they're using the same generic voice lines I've heard 1,000 times. Especially when these recorded lines rarely apply to the situation at hand. Pedestrians look impressive, but their AI is distractingly stupid. They're tempermental Skyrim NPC's with better graphics. If you walk a step too far away from them, they'll assume you're abandoning them and turn violent, or they'll try to kill you for riding your horse too closely. This system collapses under its own weight once the imprecise controls and nonsensical button-mappings are thrown into the mix. A lot of convenience and playability is sacrificed to make this world seem realistic, but it doesn't maintain that illusion well enough to justify most of those losses. Still, for as much as it takes away, it does add som…
